blocks.text: Organisms require nutrition for their survival and maintenance. A nutrient is a substance that provides the body with the essential ingredients required for metabolism. Specific nutrients such as carbohydrates, lipids and proteins serve as sources of energy; others, including water, electrolytes, minerals and vitamins, are necessary for the metabolic process. Nutrition refers to the collective processes involved in the intake and use of nutrients for growth, repair and the maintenance of activities in an organism.

All autotrophic organisms need carbon dioxide and water, which supply carbon, oxygen and hydrogen, the predominant elements required for making organic molecules. Plants get many other nutrients from the environment, and these fall into two groups. Macronutrients are needed in relatively larger amounts: there are nine, namely carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen, potassium, calcium, phosphorus, magnesium and sulphur. Micronutrients are needed in very small amounts: there are seven, namely iron, manganese, zinc, molybdenum, copper, chlorine and boron.

blocks.title: Fertilisers
blocks.text: Fertilisers are added to the soil to provide macronutrients and micronutrients to crops.

blocks.title: Manganese and stress
blocks.text: Manganese is important for the activity of antioxidant enzymes such as superoxide dismutase (SOD), which help to mitigate oxidative stress in plants under adverse environmental conditions.

Some plants supplement their food with organic molecules in addition to inorganic nutrients, acquired by capturing and breaking down insects and tiny animals. All insectivorous plants are true autotrophs, but their development accelerates when they capture prey; the nitrogenous compounds of the animal body are evidently of benefit. The captured insects are broken down by enzymes released by the leaves. The pitcher plant, Venus fly trap and sundew are well-known insectivorous plants.

items: Pitcher plant: the leaves are modified into a sac or pitcher partly filled with water. The terminal part of the leaf forms a hood that partly covers the opening, and numerous stiff hairs prevent little insects from crawling out once they have fallen in.

Venus fly trap: the trap is two lobes hinged at the end of each leaf. The inner surfaces carry trichomes, hair-like projections that trigger the lobes to close rapidly on contact with prey. Fine bristles along the hinged traps interlock on closure so the prey cannot escape; it is digested by enzymes secreted from glands on the leaf surface and the products are absorbed.

Sundew: catches prey with shiny drops of dew, from which its name comes. The leaves are covered with tiny tentacle-like hairs, each with a gland and a single drop of dew at the tip. Insects attracted by the plant's odour are trapped by the tentacles, digested by enzymes, and the products absorbed.

blocks.alt: Three schematic plants. A pitcher plant: a tall green sac with water at the bottom, a hood over its mouth and stiff hairs pointing down inside. A Venus fly trap: two hinged lobes with orange trigger hairs and marginal bristles closing on a black insect. A sundew leaf: an oval covered with orange tentacles each tipped by a blue drop.
blocks.caption: Pitcher plant, Venus fly trap and sundew (original diagram after Figures 8.1 to 8.3).
blocks.long_description: The pitcher plant's leaf is a water-filled sac with a hood and inward-pointing stiff hairs that stop insects crawling out. The Venus fly trap's leaf ends in two hinged lobes with trigger hairs on their inner faces and bristles on their rims; touching the hairs snaps the lobes shut and glands digest the prey. The sundew's leaf carries tentacle-like hairs tipped with sticky dew that hold insects attracted by the plant's odour until enzymes digest them.

blocks.prompt: A tomato plant shows dark patches on its leaves, and a maize plant has yellowing between the veins of its leaves. Which nutrient is each short of, and is it a macro- or micronutrient?
blocks.explanation: Dark patches on the leaves point to a shortage of potassium, a macronutrient involved in water regulation and transport. Interveinal chlorosis points to a shortage of iron, a micronutrient needed for chlorophyll synthesis.

items: Nutrients supply energy (carbohydrates, lipids, proteins) or support metabolism (water, electrolytes, minerals, vitamins); nutrition is their intake and use.
Nine macronutrients: C, H, O, N, K, Ca, P, Mg, S. Seven micronutrients: Fe, Mn, Zn, Mo, Cu, Cl, B. Each has a role and a deficiency sign, from stunted growth to chlorosis.
Insectivorous plants (pitcher plant, Venus fly trap, sundew) are autotrophs that gain nitrogen by trapping and digesting insects with leaf enzymes.
